newsitem.title: KAZAKHSTAN: Kazakh 3-mth T-bills to steady or edge up-dealers.
newsitem.headline: Kazakh 3-mth T-bills to steady or edge up-dealers.

text.p: The yield on Kazakh three-month treasury bills (GKOs) could remain unchanged next week or rise only slightly as investors have been attracted by the alternative of higher yields on central bank notes, dealers said on Friday.
Kazakhstan's finance ministry is offering 650 million tenge of three-month T-bills at an auction on Tuesday.
This week the yield on three-month GKOs rose to 22.52 percent annual from 21.21 percent last Tuesday.
Demand for three-month paper on Tuesday's auction was 780 million tenge, compared to demand of 2.01 billion tenge the previous week.
Dealers said the rise in yields this week reflected the fall in demand.

Oleg Tsurkan, head treasurer at ABN AMRO Bank Kazakhstan, told Reuters he expected the paper to be roughly unchanged for the next two or three weeks "given current demand which has reached its lowest point".
He said many investors were drawn to the National Bank of Kazakhstan's 18-day and 28-day notes which pay yields of 28-29 percent annually.

The central bank issues short term notes to sterilise the money supply and insure the stability of tenge exchange rates. The tenge has strengthened fairly steadily this month to 75.10 per dollar on Friday from 75.80 on February 24.
Next week, the National Bank will hold two auctions of notes worth a total of 1.75 billion tenge -- a much larger volume compared to next Tuesday's auction of 650 million tenge three-month GKOs.
"As long as notes exist, many banks would prefer to invest in them, especially given their higher yields," said Denis Fedosenko, dealer at Kazkommertsbank.
Fedosenko said that the move of many investors to notes from GKOs could lead to smaller demand for the latter, and their yield could edge up slightly, to 23-24 percent annual.
Dealers appeared confident that yields on National Bank notes would not go down sharply and would remain attractive.
"The National Bank will continue fulfilling its task of keeping the exchange rate stable, and in the market there is money the bank has to sterilise," Tsurkan said.
